## File: src/content/docs/ai-sdk/03-prompts.mdx
`````
  1: ---
  2: title: Prompts
  3: description: Learn about the Prompt structure used in the AI SDK.
  4: status: public
  5: tags: ["AI", "prompts", "LLM", "system-prompts", "messages", "content-types"]
  6: ---
  7: 
  8: # Prompts
  9: 
 10: Prompts are instructions that you give a large language model (LLM) to tell it what to do.
 11: It's like when you ask someone for directions; the clearer your question, the better the directions you'll get.
 12: 
 13: Many LLM providers offer complex interfaces for specifying prompts. They involve different roles and message types.
 14: While these interfaces are powerful, they can be hard to use and understand.
 15: 
 16: In order to simplify prompting, the AI SDK support text, message, and system prompts.
 17: 
 18: ## Text Prompts
 19: 
 20: Text prompts are strings.
 21: They are ideal for simple generation use cases,
 22: e.g. repeatedly generating content for variants of the same prompt text.
 23: 
 24: You can set text prompts using the `prompt` property made available by AI SDK functions like `streamText` or `generateObject`.
 25: You can structure the text in any way and inject variables, e.g. using a template literal.
 26: 
 27: ```ts
 28: const result = await generateText({
 29:   model: yourModel,
 30:   prompt: 'Invent a new holiday and describe its traditions.',
 31: });
 32: ```
 33: 
 34: You can also use template literals to provide dynamic data to your prompt.
 35: 
 36: ```ts
 37: const result = await generateText({
 38:   model: yourModel,
 39:   prompt:
 40:     `I am planning a trip to ${destination} for ${lengthOfStay} days. ` +
 41:     `Please suggest the best tourist activities for me to do.`,
 42: });
 43: ```
 44: 
 45: ## System Prompts
 46: 
 47: System prompts are the initial set of instructions given to models that help guide and constrain the models' behaviors and responses.
 48: You can set system prompts using the `system` property.
 49: System prompts work with both the `prompt` and the `messages` properties.
 50: 
 51: ```ts
 52: const result = await generateText({
 53:   model: yourModel,
 54:   system:
 55:     `You help planning travel itineraries. ` +
 56:     `Respond to the users' request with a list ` +
 57:     `of the best stops to make in their destination.`,
 58:   prompt:
 59:     `I am planning a trip to ${destination} for ${lengthOfStay} days. ` +
 60:     `Please suggest the best tourist activities for me to do.`,
 61: });
 62: ```
 63: 
 64: When you use a message prompt, you can also use system messages instead of a system prompt.
 65: 
 66: ## Message Prompts
 67: 
 68: A message prompt is an array of user, assistant, and tool messages.
 69: They are great for chat interfaces and more complex, multi-modal prompts.
 70: You can use the `messages` property to set message prompts.
 71: 
 72: Each message has a `role` and a `content` property. The content can either be text (for user and assistant messages), or an array of relevant parts (data) for that message type.
 73: 
 74: ```ts
 75: const result = await streamUI({
 76:   model: yourModel,
 77:   messages: [
 78:     { role: 'user', content: 'Hi!' },
 79:     { role: 'assistant', content: 'Hello, how can I help?' },
 80:     { role: 'user', content: 'Where can I buy the best Currywurst in Berlin?' },
 81:   ],
 82: });
 83: ```
 84: 
 85: Instead of sending a text in the `content` property, you can send an array of parts that includes a mix of text and other content parts.
 86: 
 87: Not all language models support all message and content types. For example, some models might not be capable of handling multi-modal inputs or tool messages.
 88: 
 89: ### User Messages
 90: 
 91: #### Text Parts
 92: 
 93: Text content is the most common type of content. It is a string that is passed to the model.
 94: 
 95: If you only need to send text content in a message, the `content` property can be a string,
 96: but you can also use it to send multiple content parts.
 97: 
 98: ```ts
 99: const result = await generateText({
100:   model: yourModel,
101:   messages: [
102:     {
103:       role: 'user',
104:       content: [
105:         {
106:           type: 'text',
107:           text: 'Where can I buy the best Currywurst in Berlin?',
108:         },
109:       ],
110:     },
111:   ],
112: });
113: ```
114: 
115: #### Image Parts
116: 
117: User messages can include image parts. An image can be one of the following:
118: 
119: - base64-encoded image:
120:   - `string` with base-64 encoded content
121:   - data URL `string`, e.g. `data:image/png;base64,...`
122: - binary image:
123:   - `ArrayBuffer`
124:   - `Uint8Array`
125:   - `Buffer`
126: - URL:
127:   - http(s) URL `string`, e.g. `https://example.com/image.png`
128:   - `URL` object, e.g. `new URL('https://example.com/image.png')`
129: 
130: ##### Example: Binary image (Buffer)
131: 
132: ```ts
133: const result = await generateText({
134:   model,
135:   messages: [
136:     {
137:       role: 'user',
138:       content: [
139:         { type: 'text', text: 'Describe the image in detail.' },
140:         {
141:           type: 'image',
142:           image: fs.readFileSync('./data/comic-cat.png'),
143:         },
144:       ],
145:     },
146:   ],
147: });
148: ```
149: 
150: ##### Example: Base-64 encoded image (string)
151: 
152: ```ts
153: const result = await generateText({
154:   model: yourModel,
155:   messages: [
156:     {
157:       role: 'user',
158:       content: [
159:         { type: 'text', text: 'Describe the image in detail.' },
160:         {
161:           type: 'image',
162:           image: fs.readFileSync('./data/comic-cat.png').toString('base64'),
163:         },
164:       ],
165:     },
166:   ],
167: });
168: ```
169: 
170: ##### Example: Image URL (string)
171: 
172: ```ts
173: const result = await generateText({
174:   model: yourModel,
175:   messages: [
176:     {
177:       role: 'user',
178:       content: [
179:         { type: 'text', text: 'Describe the image in detail.' },
180:         {
181:           type: 'image',
182:           image: 'https://example.com/comic-cat.png',
183:         },
184:       ],
185:     },
186:   ],
187: });
188: ```
189: 
190: #### File Parts
191: 
192: Only a few providers and models currently support file parts from specific providers for specific file types like wav, mp3 audio, and pdf files.
193: 
194: User messages can include file parts. A file can be one of the following:
195: 
196: - base64-encoded file:
197:   - `string` with base-64 encoded content
198:   - data URL `string`, e.g. `data:image/png;base64,...`
199: - binary data:
200:   - `ArrayBuffer`
201:   - `Uint8Array`
202:   - `Buffer`
203: - URL:
204:   - http(s) URL `string`, e.g. `https://example.com/some.pdf`
205:   - `URL` object, e.g. `new URL('https://example.com/some.pdf')`
206: 
207: You need to specify the MIME type of the file you are sending.
208: 
209: ##### Example: PDF file from Buffer
210: 
211: ```ts
212: const result = await generateText({
213:   model: yourModel,
214:   messages: [
215:     {
216:       role: 'user',
217:       content: [
218:         { type: 'text', text: 'What is the file about?' },
219:         {
220:           type: 'file',
221:           mimeType: 'application/pdf',
222:           data: fs.readFileSync('./data/example.pdf'),
223:         },
224:       ],
225:     },
226:   ],
227: });
228: ```
229: 
230: ##### Example: mp3 audio file from Buffer
231: 
232: ```ts
233: const result = await generateText({
234:   model: yourModel,
235:   messages: [
236:     {
237:       role: 'user',
238:       content: [
239:         { type: 'text', text: 'What is the audio saying?' },
240:         {
241:           type: 'file',
242:           mimeType: 'audio/mpeg',
243:           data: fs.readFileSync('./data/audio.mp3'),
244:         },
245:       ],
246:     },
247:   ],
248: });
249: ```
250: 
251: ### Assistant Messages
252: 
253: Assistant messages are messages that have a role of `assistant`.
254: They are typically previous responses from the assistant
255: and can contain text, reasoning, and tool call parts.
256: 
257: #### Example: Assistant message with text content
258: 
259: ```ts
260: const result = await generateText({
261:   model: yourModel,
262:   messages: [
263:     { role: 'user', content: 'Hi!' },
264:     { role: 'assistant', content: 'Hello, how can I help?' },
265:   ],
266: });
267: ```
268: 
269: #### Example: Assistant message with text content in array
270: 
271: ```ts
272: const result = await generateText({
273:   model: yourModel,
274:   messages: [
275:     { role: 'user', content: 'Hi!' },
276:     {
277:       role: 'assistant',
278:       content: [{ type: 'text', text: 'Hello, how can I help?' }],
279:     },
280:   ],
281: });
282: ```
283: 
284: #### Example: Assistant message with tool call content
285: 
286: ```ts
287: const result = await generateText({
288:   model: yourModel,
289:   messages: [
290:     { role: 'user', content: 'How many calories are in this block of cheese?' },
291:     {
292:       role: 'assistant',
293:       content: [
294:         {
295:           type: 'tool-call',
296:           toolCallId: '12345',
297:           toolName: 'get-nutrition-data',
298:           args: { cheese: 'Roquefort' },
299:         },
300:       ],
301:     },
302:   ],
303: });
304: ```
305: 
306: ### Tool messages
307: 
308: Tools (also known as function calling) are programs that you can provide an LLM to extend its built-in functionality. This can be anything from calling an external API to calling functions within your UI.
309: 
310: For models that support tool calls, assistant messages can contain tool call parts, and tool messages can contain tool result parts.
311: A single assistant message can call multiple tools, and a single tool message can contain multiple tool results.
312: 
313: ```ts
314: const result = await generateText({
315:   model: yourModel,
316:   messages: [
317:     {
318:       role: 'user',
319:       content: [
320:         {
321:           type: 'text',
322:           text: 'How many calories are in this block of cheese?',
323:         },
324:         { type: 'image', image: fs.readFileSync('./data/roquefort.jpg') },
325:       ],
326:     },
327:     {
328:       role: 'assistant',
329:       content: [
330:         {
331:           type: 'tool-call',
332:           toolCallId: '12345',
333:           toolName: 'get-nutrition-data',
334:           args: { cheese: 'Roquefort' },
335:         },
336:       ],
337:     },
338:     {
339:       role: 'tool',
340:       content: [
341:         {
342:           type: 'tool-result',
343:           toolCallId: '12345',
344:           toolName: 'get-nutrition-data',
345:           result: {
346:             name: 'Cheese, roquefort',
347:             calories: 369,
348:             fat: 31,
349:             protein: 22,
350:           },
351:         },
352:       ],
353:     },
354:   ],
355: });
356: ```
357: 
358: #### Multi-modal Tool Results
359: 
360: Multi-part tool results are experimental and only supported by specific providers.
361: 
362: Tool results can be multi-part and multi-modal, e.g. a text and an image.
363: You can use the `experimental_content` property on tool parts to specify multi-part tool results.
364: 
365: ```ts
366: const result = await generateText({
367:   model: yourModel,
368:   messages: [
369:     {
370:       role: 'tool',
371:       content: [
372:         {
373:           type: 'tool-result',
374:           toolCallId: '12345',
375:           toolName: 'get-nutrition-data',
376:           result: {
377:             name: 'Cheese, roquefort',
378:             calories: 369,
379:             fat: 31,
380:             protein: 22,
381:           },
382:           content: [
383:             {
384:               type: 'text',
385:               text: 'Here is an image of the nutrition data for the cheese:',
386:             },
387:             {
388:               type: 'image',
389:               data: fs.readFileSync('./data/nutrition-data.png'),
390:               mimeType: 'image/png',
391:             },
392:           ],
393:         },
394:       ],
395:     },
396:   ],
397: });
398: ```
399: 
400: ### System Messages
401: 
402: System messages are messages that are sent to the model before the user messages to guide the assistant's behavior.
403: You can alternatively use the `system` property.
404: 
405: ```ts
406: const result = await generateText({
407:   model: yourModel,
408:   messages: [
409:     { role: 'system', content: 'You help planning travel itineraries.' },
410:     {
411:       role: 'user',
412:       content:
413:         'I am planning a trip to Berlin for 3 days. Please suggest the best tourist activities for me to do.',
414:     },
415:   ],
416: });
`````

## File: src/content/docs/ai-sdk/04-tools.mdx
`````
 1: ---
 2: title: Tools
 3: description: Learn about tools with the AI SDK.
 4: status: public
 5: tags: ["AI", "tools", "LLM", "integrations", "toolkits", "schemas"]
 6: ---
 7: 
 8: # Tools
 9: 
10: While large language models (LLMs) have incredible generation capabilities,
11: they struggle with discrete tasks (e.g. mathematics) and interacting with the outside world (e.g. getting the weather).
12: 
13: Tools are actions that an LLM can invoke.
14: The results of these actions can be reported back to the LLM to be considered in the next response.
15: 
16: For example, when you ask an LLM for the "weather in London", and there is a weather tool available, it could call a tool
17: with London as the argument. The tool would then fetch the weather data and return it to the LLM. The LLM can then use this
18: information in its response.
19: 
20: ## What is a tool?
21: 
22: A tool is an object that can be called by the model to perform a specific task.
23: You can use tools with `generateText` and `streamText` by passing one or more tools to the `tools` parameter.
24: 
25: A tool consists of three properties:
26: 
27: - **`description`**: An optional description of the tool that can influence when the tool is picked.
28: - **`parameters`**: A Zod schema or a JSON schema that defines the parameters. The schema is consumed by the LLM, and also used to validate the LLM tool calls.
29: - **`execute`**: An optional async function that is called with the arguments from the tool call.
30: 
31: If the LLM decides to use a tool, it will generate a tool call.
32: Tools with an `execute` function are run automatically when these calls are generated.
33: The results of the tool calls are returned using tool result objects.
34: 
35: You can automatically pass tool results back to the LLM using multi-step calls with `streamText` and `generateText`.
36: 
37: ## Schemas
38: 
39: Schemas are used to define the parameters for tools and to validate the tool calls.
40: 
41: The AI SDK supports both raw JSON schemas (using the `jsonSchema` function)
42: and [Zod](https://zod.dev/) schemas (either directly or using the `zodSchema` function).
43: 
44: [Zod](https://zod.dev/) is a popular TypeScript schema validation library.
45: You can install it with:
46: 
47: ```bash
48: # Using pnpm
49: pnpm add zod
50: 
51: # Using npm
52: npm install zod
53: 
54: # Using yarn
55: yarn add zod
56: ```
57: 
58: You can then specify a Zod schema, for example:
59: 
60: ```ts
61: import z from 'zod';
62: 
63: const recipeSchema = z.object({
64:   recipe: z.object({
65:     name: z.string(),
66:     ingredients: z.array(
67:       z.object({
68:         name: z.string(),
69:         amount: z.string(),
70:       }),
71:     ),
72:     steps: z.array(z.string()),
73:   }),
74: });
75: ```
76: 
77: You can also use schemas for structured output generation with `generateObject` and `streamObject`.
78: 
79: ## Toolkits
80: 
81: When you work with tools, you typically need a mix of application specific tools and general purpose tools.
82: There are several providers that offer pre-built tools as **toolkits** that you can use out of the box:
83: 
84: - **[agentic](https://github.com/transitive-bullshit/agentic)** - A collection of 20+ tools. Most tools connect to access external APIs such as [Exa](https://exa.ai/) or [E2B](https://e2b.dev/).
85: - **[browserbase](https://docs.browserbase.com/integrations/vercel-ai/introduction)** - Browser tool that runs a headless browser
86: - **[Stripe agent tools](https://docs.stripe.com/agents)** - Tools for interacting with Stripe.
87: - **[Toolhouse](https://docs.toolhouse.ai/toolhouse/using-vercel-ai)** - AI function-calling in 3 lines of code for over 25 different actions.
88: - **[Agent Tools](https://ai-sdk-agents.vercel.app/?item=introduction)** - A collection of tools for agents.
89: - **[AI Tool Maker](https://github.com/nihaocami/ai-tool-maker)** - A CLI utility to generate AI SDK tools from OpenAPI specs.
90: - **[Composio](https://docs.composio.dev/javascript/vercel)** - Composio provides 250+ tools like GitHub, Gmail, Salesforce and [more](https://composio.dev/tools).
91: 
92: ## Learn more
93: 
94: The AI SDK Core Tool Calling and Agents documentation has more information about tools and tool calling.
`````

`````
 1: ---
 2: title: Streaming
 3: description: Why use streaming for AI applications?
 4: status: public
 5: tags: ["AI", "streaming", "LLM", "UX", "performance", "real-time"]
 6: ---
 7: 
 8: # Streaming
 9: 
10: Streaming conversational text UIs (like ChatGPT) have gained massive popularity over the past few months. This section explores the benefits and drawbacks of streaming and blocking interfaces.
11: 
12: Large language models (LLMs) are extremely powerful. However, when generating long outputs, they can be very slow compared to the latency you're likely used to. If you try to build a traditional blocking UI, your users might easily find themselves staring at loading spinners for 5, 10, even up to 40s waiting for the entire LLM response to be generated. This can lead to a poor user experience, especially in conversational applications like chatbots. Streaming UIs can help mitigate this issue by **displaying parts of the response as they become available**.
13: 
14: ### Streaming UI
15: 
16: While streaming interfaces can greatly enhance user experiences, especially with larger language models, they aren't always necessary or beneficial. If you can achieve your desired functionality using a smaller, faster model without resorting to streaming, this route can often lead to simpler and more manageable development processes.
17: 
18: However, regardless of the speed of your model, the AI SDK is designed to make implementing streaming UIs as simple as possible. In the example below, we stream text generation from OpenAI's `gpt-4-turbo` in under 10 lines of code using the SDK's `streamText` function:
19: 
20: ```ts
21: import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
22: import { streamText } from 'ai';
23: 
24: const { textStream } = streamText({
25:   model: openai('gpt-4-turbo'),
26:   prompt: 'Write a poem about embedding models.',
27: });
28: 
29: for await (const textPart of textStream) {
30:   console.log(textPart);
31: }
32: ```
33: 
34: For an introduction to streaming UIs and the AI SDK, check out our Getting Started guides.
`````

## File: src/content/docs/ai-sdk/06-agents.mdx
`````
  1: ---
  2: title: Agents
  3: description: Learn how to build agents with AI SDK Core.
  4: status: public
  5: tags: ["AI", "agents", "LLM", "tools", "workflows", "orchestration", "patterns"]
  6: ---
  7: 
  8: # Agents
  9: 
 10: When building AI applications, you often need **systems that can understand context and take meaningful actions**. When building these systems, the key consideration is finding the right balance between flexibility and control. Let's explore different approaches and patterns for building these systems, with a focus on helping you match capabilities to your needs.
 11: 
 12: ## Building Blocks
 13: 
 14: When building AI systems, you can combine these fundamental components:
 15: 
 16: ### Single-Step LLM Generation
 17: 
 18: The basic building block - one call to an LLM to get a response. Useful for straightforward tasks like classification or text generation.
 19: 
 20: ### Tool Usage
 21: 
 22: Enhanced capabilities through tools (like calculators, APIs, or databases) that the LLM can use to accomplish tasks. Tools provide a controlled way to extend what the LLM can do.
 23: 
 24: When solving complex problems, **an LLM can make multiple tool calls across multiple steps without you explicitly specifying the order** - for example, looking up information in a database, using that to make calculations, and then storing results. The AI SDK makes this multi-step tool usage straightforward through the `maxSteps` parameter.
 25: 
 26: ### Multi-Agent Systems
 27: 
 28: Multiple LLMs working together, each specialized for different aspects of a complex task. This enables sophisticated behaviors while keeping individual components focused.
 29: 
 30: ## Patterns
 31: 
 32: These building blocks can be combined with workflow patterns that help manage complexity:
 33: 
 34: - Sequential Processing - Steps executed in order
 35: - Parallel Processing - Independent tasks run simultaneously
 36: - Evaluation/Feedback Loops - Results checked and improved iteratively
 37: - Orchestration - Coordinating multiple components
 38: - Routing - Directing work based on context
 39: 
 40: ## Choosing Your Approach
 41: 
 42: The key factors to consider:
 43: 
 44: - **Flexibility vs Control** - How much freedom does the LLM need vs how tightly must you constrain its actions?
 45: - **Error Tolerance** - What are the consequences of mistakes in your use case?
 46: - **Cost Considerations** - More complex systems typically mean more LLM calls and higher costs
 47: - **Maintenance** - Simpler architectures are easier to debug and modify
 48: 
 49: **Start with the simplest approach that meets your needs**. Add complexity only when required by:
 50: 
 51: 1. Breaking down tasks into clear steps
 52: 2. Adding tools for specific capabilities
 53: 3. Implementing feedback loops for quality control
 54: 4. Introducing multiple agents for complex workflows
 55: 
 56: Let's look at examples of these patterns in action.
 57: 
 58: ## Patterns with Examples
 59: 
 60: The following patterns serve as building blocks that can be combined to create comprehensive workflows. Each pattern addresses specific aspects of task execution, and by combining them thoughtfully, you can build reliable solutions for complex problems.
 61: 
 62: ### Sequential Processing (Chains)
 63: 
 64: The simplest workflow pattern executes steps in a predefined order. Each step's output becomes input for the next step, creating a clear chain of operations. This pattern is ideal for tasks with well-defined sequences, like content generation pipelines or data transformation processes.
 65: 
 66: ```ts
 67: import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
 68: import { generateText, generateObject } from 'ai';
 69: import { z } from 'zod';
 70: 
 71: async function generateMarketingCopy(input: string) {
 72:   const model = openai('gpt-4o');
 73: 
 74:   // First step: Generate marketing copy
 75:   const { text: copy } = await generateText({
 76:     model,
 77:     prompt: `Write persuasive marketing copy for: ${input}. Focus on benefits and emotional appeal.`,
 78:   });
 79: 
 80:   // Perform quality check on copy
 81:   const { object: qualityMetrics } = await generateObject({
 82:     model,
 83:     schema: z.object({
 84:       hasCallToAction: z.boolean(),
 85:       emotionalAppeal: z.number().min(1).max(10),
 86:       clarity: z.number().min(1).max(10),
 87:     }),
 88:     prompt: `Evaluate this marketing copy for:
 89:     1. Presence of call to action (true/false)
 90:     2. Emotional appeal (1-10)
 91:     3. Clarity (1-10)
 92: 
 93:     Copy to evaluate: ${copy}`,
 94:   });
 95: 
 96:   // If quality check fails, regenerate with more specific instructions
 97:   if (
 98:     !qualityMetrics.hasCallToAction ||
 99:     qualityMetrics.emotionalAppeal < 7 ||
100:     qualityMetrics.clarity < 7
101:   ) {
102:     const { text: improvedCopy } = await generateText({
103:       model,
104:       prompt: `Rewrite this marketing copy with:
105:       ${!qualityMetrics.hasCallToAction ? '- A clear call to action' : ''}
106:       ${qualityMetrics.emotionalAppeal < 7 ? '- Stronger emotional appeal' : ''}
107:       ${qualityMetrics.clarity < 7 ? '- Improved clarity and directness' : ''}
108: 
109:       Original copy: ${copy}`,
110:     });
111:     return { copy: improvedCopy, qualityMetrics };
112:   }
113: 
114:   return { copy, qualityMetrics };
115: }
116: ```
117: 
118: ### Routing
119: 
120: This pattern allows the model to make decisions about which path to take through a workflow based on context and intermediate results. The model acts as an intelligent router, directing the flow of execution between different branches of your workflow. This is particularly useful when handling varied inputs that require different processing approaches.
121: 
122: ```ts
123: import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
124: import { generateObject, generateText } from 'ai';
125: import { z } from 'zod';
126: 
127: async function handleCustomerQuery(query: string) {
128:   const model = openai('gpt-4o');
129: 
130:   // First step: Classify the query type
131:   const { object: classification } = await generateObject({
132:     model,
133:     schema: z.object({
134:       reasoning: z.string(),
135:       type: z.enum(['general', 'refund', 'technical']),
136:       complexity: z.enum(['simple', 'complex']),
137:     }),
138:     prompt: `Classify this customer query:
139:     ${query}
140: 
141:     Determine:
142:     1. Query type (general, refund, or technical)
143:     2. Complexity (simple or complex)
144:     3. Brief reasoning for classification`,
145:   });
146: 
147:   // Route based on classification
148:   const { text: response } = await generateText({
149:     model:
150:       classification.complexity === 'simple'
151:         ? openai('gpt-4o-mini')
152:         : openai('o3-mini'),
153:     system: {
154:       general:
155:         'You are an expert customer service agent handling general inquiries.',
156:       refund:
157:         'You are a customer service agent specializing in refund requests. Follow company policy and collect necessary information.',
158:       technical:
159:         'You are a technical support specialist with deep product knowledge. Focus on clear step-by-step troubleshooting.',
160:     }[classification.type],
161:     prompt: query,
162:   });
163: 
164:   return { response, classification };
165: }
166: ```
167: 
168: ### Parallel Processing
169: 
170: Some tasks can be broken down into independent subtasks that can be executed simultaneously. This pattern takes advantage of parallel execution to improve efficiency while maintaining the benefits of structured workflows.
171: 
172: ```ts
173: import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
174: import { generateText, generateObject } from 'ai';
175: import { z } from 'zod';
176: 
177: async function parallelCodeReview(code: string) {
178:   const model = openai('gpt-4o');
179: 
180:   // Run parallel reviews
181:   const [securityReview, performanceReview, maintainabilityReview] =
182:     await Promise.all([
183:       generateObject({
184:         model,
185:         system:
186:           'You are an expert in code security. Focus on identifying security vulnerabilities, injection risks, and authentication issues.',
187:         schema: z.object({
188:           vulnerabilities: z.array(z.string()),
189:           riskLevel: z.enum(['low', 'medium', 'high']),
190:           suggestions: z.array(z.string()),
191:         }),
192:         prompt: `Review this code:
193:       ${code}`,
194:       }),
195: 
196:       generateObject({
197:         model,
198:         system:
199:           'You are an expert in code performance. Focus on identifying performance bottlenecks, memory leaks, and optimization opportunities.',
200:         schema: z.object({
201:           issues: z.array(z.string()),
202:           impact: z.enum(['low', 'medium', 'high']),
203:           optimizations: z.array(z.string()),
204:         }),
205:         prompt: `Review this code:
206:       ${code}`,
207:       }),
208: 
209:       generateObject({
210:         model,
211:         system:
212:           'You are an expert in code quality. Focus on code structure, readability, and adherence to best practices.',
213:         schema: z.object({
214:           concerns: z.array(z.string()),
215:           qualityScore: z.number().min(1).max(10),
216:           recommendations: z.array(z.string()),
217:         }),
218:         prompt: `Review this code:
219:       ${code}`,
220:       }),
221:     ]);
222: 
223:   const reviews = [
224:     { ...securityReview.object, type: 'security' },
225:     { ...performanceReview.object, type: 'performance' },
226:     { ...maintainabilityReview.object, type: 'maintainability' },
227:   ];
228: 
229:   // Aggregate results using another model instance
230:   const { text: summary } = await generateText({
231:     model,
232:     system: 'You are a technical lead summarizing multiple code reviews.',
233:     prompt: `Synthesize these code review results into a concise summary with key actions:
234:     ${JSON.stringify(reviews, null, 2)}`,
235:   });
236: 
237:   return { reviews, summary };
238: }
239: ```
240: 
241: ### Orchestrator-Worker
242: 
243: In this pattern, a primary model (orchestrator) coordinates the execution of specialized workers. Each worker is optimized for a specific subtask, while the orchestrator maintains overall context and ensures coherent results.
244: 
245: ```ts
246: import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
247: import { generateObject } from 'ai';
248: import { z } from 'zod';
249: 
250: async function implementFeature(featureRequest: string) {
251:   // Orchestrator: Plan the implementation
252:   const { object: implementationPlan } = await generateObject({
253:     model: openai('o3-mini'),
254:     schema: z.object({
255:       files: z.array(
256:         z.object({
257:           purpose: z.string(),
258:           filePath: z.string(),
259:           changeType: z.enum(['create', 'modify', 'delete']),
260:         }),
261:       ),
262:       estimatedComplexity: z.enum(['low', 'medium', 'high']),
263:     }),
264:     system:
265:       'You are a senior software architect planning feature implementations.',
266:     prompt: `Analyze this feature request and create an implementation plan:
267:     ${featureRequest}`,
268:   });
269: 
270:   // Workers: Execute the planned changes
271:   const fileChanges = await Promise.all(
272:     implementationPlan.files.map(async file => {
273:       const workerSystemPrompt = {
274:         create:
275:           'You are an expert at implementing new files following best practices and project patterns.',
276:         modify:
277:           'You are an expert at modifying existing code while maintaining consistency and avoiding regressions.',
278:         delete:
279:           'You are an expert at safely removing code while ensuring no breaking changes.',
280:       }[file.changeType];
281: 
282:       const { object: change } = await generateObject({
283:         model: openai('gpt-4o'),
284:         schema: z.object({
285:           explanation: z.string(),
286:           code: z.string(),
287:         }),
288:         system: workerSystemPrompt,
289:         prompt: `Implement the changes for ${file.filePath} to support:
290:         ${file.purpose}
291: 
292:         Consider the overall feature context:
293:         ${featureRequest}`,
294:       });
295: 
296:       return {
297:         file,
298:         implementation: change,
299:       };
300:     }),
301:   );
302: 
303:   return {
304:     plan: implementationPlan,
305:     changes: fileChanges,
306:   };
307: }
308: ```
309: 
310: ### Evaluator-Optimizer
311: 
312: This pattern introduces quality control into workflows by having dedicated evaluation steps that assess intermediate results. Based on the evaluation, the workflow can either proceed, retry with adjusted parameters, or take corrective action.
313: 
314: ```ts
315: import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
316: import { generateText, generateObject } from 'ai';
317: import { z } from 'zod';
318: 
319: async function translateWithFeedback(text: string, targetLanguage: string) {
320:   let currentTranslation = '';
321:   let iterations = 0;
322:   const MAX_ITERATIONS = 3;
323: 
324:   // Initial translation
325:   const { text: translation } = await generateText({
326:     model: openai('gpt-4o-mini'),
327:     system: 'You are an expert literary translator.',
328:     prompt: `Translate this text to ${targetLanguage}, preserving tone and cultural nuances:
329:     ${text}`,
330:   });
331: 
332:   currentTranslation = translation;
333: 
334:   // Evaluation-optimization loop
335:   while (iterations < MAX_ITERATIONS) {
336:     // Evaluate current translation
337:     const { object: evaluation } = await generateObject({
338:       model: openai('gpt-4o'),
339:       schema: z.object({
340:         qualityScore: z.number().min(1).max(10),
341:         preservesTone: z.boolean(),
342:         preservesNuance: z.boolean(),
343:         culturallyAccurate: z.boolean(),
344:         specificIssues: z.array(z.string()),
345:         improvementSuggestions: z.array(z.string()),
346:       }),
347:       system: 'You are an expert in evaluating literary translations.',
348:       prompt: `Evaluate this translation:
349: 
350:       Original: ${text}
351:       Translation: ${currentTranslation}
352: 
353:       Consider:
354:       1. Overall quality
355:       2. Preservation of tone
356:       3. Preservation of nuance
357:       4. Cultural accuracy`,
358:     });
359: 
360:     // Check if quality meets threshold
361:     if (
362:       evaluation.qualityScore >= 8 &&
363:       evaluation.preservesTone &&
364:       evaluation.preservesNuance &&
365:       evaluation.culturallyAccurate
366:     ) {
367:       break;
368:     }
369: 
370:     // Generate improved translation based on feedback
371:     const { text: improvedTranslation } = await generateText({
372:       model: openai('gpt-4o'),
373:       system: 'You are an expert literary translator.',
374:       prompt: `Improve this translation based on the following feedback:
375:       ${evaluation.specificIssues.join('\n')}
376:       ${evaluation.improvementSuggestions.join('\n')}
377: 
378:       Original: ${text}
379:       Current Translation: ${currentTranslation}`,
380:     });
381: 
382:     currentTranslation = improvedTranslation;
383:     iterations++;
384:   }
385: 
386:   return {
387:     finalTranslation: currentTranslation,
388:     iterationsRequired: iterations,
389:   };
390: }
391: ```
392: 
393: ## Multi-Step Tool Usage
394: 
395: If your use case involves solving problems where the solution path is poorly defined or too complex to map out as a workflow in advance, you may want to provide the LLM with a set of lower-level tools and allow it to break down the task into small pieces that it can solve on its own iteratively, without discrete instructions. The AI SDK makes this simple with the `maxSteps` parameter.
396: 
397: With `maxSteps`, the AI SDK automatically triggers an additional request to the model after every tool result (each request is considered a "step"). If the model does not generate a tool call or the `maxSteps` threshold has been met, the generation is complete.
398: 
399: ### Using maxSteps
400: 
401: This example demonstrates how to create an agent that solves math problems using a calculator tool:
402: 
403: ```ts
404: import { openai } from '@ai-sdk/openai';
405: import { generateText, tool } from 'ai';
406: import * as mathjs from 'mathjs';
407: import { z } from 'zod';
408: 
409: const { text: answer } = await generateText({
410:   model: openai('gpt-4o-2024-08-06', { structuredOutputs: true }),
411:   tools: {
412:     calculate: tool({
413:       description:
414:         'A tool for evaluating mathematical expressions.',
415:       parameters: z.object({ expression: z.string() }),
416:       execute: async ({ expression }) => mathjs.evaluate(expression),
417:     }),
418:   },
419:   maxSteps: 10,
420:   system:
421:     'You are solving math problems. ' +
422:     'Reason step by step. ' +
423:     'Use the calculator when necessary. ' +
424:     'When you give the final answer, ' +
425:     'provide an explanation for how you arrived at it.',
426:   prompt:
427:     'A taxi driver earns $9461 per 1-hour of work. ' +
428:     'If he works 12 hours a day and in 1 hour ' +
429:     'he uses 12 liters of petrol with a price of $134 for 1 liter. ' +
430:     'How much money does he earn in one day?',
431: });
432: ```
433: 
434: ### Accessing all steps
435: 
436: Calling `generateText` with `maxSteps` can result in several calls to the LLM (steps).
437: You can access information from all steps by using the `steps` property of the response.
438: 
439: ```ts
440: import { generateText } from 'ai';
441: 
442: const { steps } = await generateText({
443:   model: openai('gpt-4o'),
444:   maxSteps: 10,
445:   // ...
446: });
447: 
448: // extract all tool calls from the steps:
449: const allToolCalls = steps.flatMap(step => step.toolCalls);
450: ```
451: 
452: ### Getting notified on each completed step
453: 
454: You can use the `onStepFinish` callback to get notified on each completed step.
455: It is triggered when a step is finished, i.e., all text deltas, tool calls, and tool results for the step are available.
456: 
457: ```ts
458: import { generateText } from 'ai';
459: 
460: const result = await generateText({
461:   model: yourModel,
462:   maxSteps: 10,
`````

## File: src/content/docs/deployment/_production.md
`````markdown
  1: ---
  2: title: Production Deployment
  3: description: Learn how to deploy ONE applications to production environments
  4: date: 2024-02-02
  5: section: Deployment
  6: order: 1
  7: ---
  8: 
  9: # Deploying to Production
 10: 
 11: This guide covers everything you need to know about deploying ONE applications to production environments, including setup, optimization, and monitoring.
 12: 
 13: ## Deployment Options
 14: 
 15: ### 1. Vercel 
 16: 
 17: The simplest way to deploy your ONE application:
 18: 
 19: ```bash
 20: # Install Vercel CLI
 21: pnpm add -g vercel
 22: 
 23: # Deploy
 24: vercel deploy
 25: ```
 26: 
 27: #### Environment Setup
 28: ```env
 29: # .env.production
 30: OPENAI_API_KEY=your_production_key
 31: EDGE_CONFIG=your_edge_config
 32: ```
 33: 
 34: #### Configuration
 35: ```typescript
 36: // vercel.json
 37: {
 38:   "regions": ["all"],
 39:   "env": {
 40:     "EDGE_RUNTIME": "1"
 41:   },
 42:   "buildCommand": "pnpm build",
 43:   "outputDirectory": "dist"
 44: }
 45: ```
 46: 
 47: ### 2. Cloudflare Pages
 48: 
 49: Note: This is under development 
 50: 
 51: ```bash
 52: # Install Wrangler
 53: pnpm add -g wrangler
 54: 
 55: # Deploy
 56: wrangler deploy
 57: ```
 58: 
 59: #### Configuration
 60: ```toml
 61: # wrangler.toml
 62: name = "your-one-app"
 63: type = "webpack"
 64: account_id = "your_account_id"
 65: workers_dev = true
 66: route = "your-domain.com/*"
 67: zone_id = "your_zone_id"
 68: 
 69: [env.production]
 70: vars = { ENVIRONMENT = "production" }
 71: ```
 72: 
 73: ### 3. Asset Optimization
 74: 
 75: ```typescript
 76: // astro.config.mjs
 77: import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config';
 78: 
 79: export default defineConfig({
 80:   build: {
 81:     inlineStylesheets: 'auto',
 82:     minify: true,
 83:     splitting: true,
 84:   },
 85:   image: {
 86:     service: 'astro/assets/services/sharp',
 87:   },
 88: });
 89: ```
 90: 
 91: ## Security Measures
 92: 
 93: ### 1. Environment Variables
 94: 
 95: ```typescript
 96: // src/env.ts
 97: import { z } from 'zod';
 98: 
 99: const envSchema = z.object({
100:   OPENAI_API_KEY: z.string().min(1),
101:   DATABASE_URL: z.string().url(),
102:   NODE_ENV: z.enum(['development', 'production', 'test']),
103: });
104: 
105: export const env = envSchema.parse(process.env);
106: ```
107: 
108: ### 3. Content Security Policy
109: 
110: ```typescript
111: // src/middleware/security.ts
112: export const securityHeaders = {
113:   'Content-Security-Policy': `
114:     default-src 'self';
115:     script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' 'unsafe-eval';
116:     style-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline';
117:     img-src 'self' blob: data:;
118:     font-src 'self';
119:     object-src 'none';
120:     base-uri 'self';
121:     form-action 'self';
122:     frame-ancestors 'none';
123:     block-all-mixed-content;
124:     upgrade-insecure-requests;
125:   `.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim(),
126:   'X-Frame-Options': 'DENY',
127:   'X-Content-Type-Options': 'nosniff',
128:   'X-XSS-Protection': '1; mode=block',
129:   'Referrer-Policy': 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin',
130:   'Permissions-Policy': 'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()'
131: };
132: ```
133: 
134: ## Monitoring
135: 
136: ### 1. Error Tracking
137: 
138: ```typescript
139: // src/lib/errorTracking.ts
140: import * as Sentry from '@sentry/node';
141: 
142: Sentry.init({
143:   dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN,
144:   environment: process.env.NODE_ENV,
145:   tracesSampleRate: 1.0,
146: });
147: 
148: export const trackError = (error: Error, context?: any) => {
149:   Sentry.captureException(error, {
150:     extra: context
151:   });
152: };
153: ```
154: 
155: ### 2. Performance Monitoring
156: 
157: ```typescript
158: // src/lib/metrics.ts
159: import { Metrics } from '@opentelemetry/api';
160: 
161: export const metrics = {
162:   chatLatency: new Metrics.Counter('chat_latency', {
163:     description: 'Chat response latency in milliseconds'
164:   }),
165:   requestCount: new Metrics.Counter('request_count', {
166:     description: 'Total number of requests'
167:   })
168: };
169: 
170: // Usage
171: metrics.chatLatency.add(responseTime);
172: metrics.requestCount.add(1);
173: ```
174: 
175: ## Health Checks
176: 
177: ```typescript
178: // src/pages/api/health.ts
179: export async function GET() {
180:   const checks = {
181:     database: await checkDatabase(),
182:     redis: await checkRedis(),
183:     openai: await checkOpenAI()
184:   };
185: 
186:   const isHealthy = Object.values(checks).every(status => status === 'healthy');
187: 
188:   return new Response(JSON.stringify({
189:     status: isHealthy ? 'healthy' : 'unhealthy',
190:     checks,
191:     timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
192:   }), {
193:     status: isHealthy ? 200 : 503,
194:     headers: {
195:       'Content-Type': 'application/json'
196:     }
197:   });
198: }
199: ```
200: 
201: ## Scaling Considerations
202: 
203: 1. **Database Connections**
204:    - Use connection pooling
205:    - Implement retry logic
206:    - Monitor connection limits
207: 
208: 2. **Memory Management**
209:    - Implement proper garbage collection
210:    - Monitor memory usage
211:    - Use streaming for large responses
212: 
213: 3. **Load Balancing**
214:    - Distribute traffic evenly
215:    - Handle failover scenarios
216:    - Monitor server health
217: 
218: ## Troubleshooting
219: 
220: ### Common Issues
221: 
222: 1. **Build Failures**
223:    ```bash
224:    # Clear cache and dependencies
225:    pnpm clean
226:    rm -rf node_modules
227:    pnpm install
228:    ```
229: 
230: 2. **API Issues**
231:    - Verify environment variables
232:    - Check API key permissions
233:    - Monitor rate limits
234: 
235: 3. **Performance Problems**
236:    - Enable edge functions
237:    - Implement caching
238:    - Optimize assets
239:    - Monitor response times
240: 
241: ## Deployment Checklist
242: 
243: - [ ] Environment variables configured
244: - [ ] Build process verified
245: - [ ] Security headers implemented
246: - [ ] Rate limiting enabled
247: - [ ] Error tracking setup
248: - [ ] Performance monitoring active
249: - [ ] Health checks configured
250: - [ ] Backup strategy in place
251: - [ ] SSL certificates installed
252: - [ ] DNS records updated
`````

## File: src/content/docs/development/chat-system.md
`````markdown
  1: ---
  2: title: Chat System Architecture
  3: description: Deep dive into ONE's AI-powered chat system architecture
  4: date: 2024-02-02
  5: section: Core Features
  6: order: 1
  7: ---
  8: 
  9: # Chat System Architecture
 10: 
 11: ONE's chat system combines Astro's static site generation with dynamic AI capabilities to create powerful, flexible chat interfaces. This guide explains the core architecture and components.
 12: 
 13: ## System Overview
 14: 
 15: ```mermaid
 16: graph TB
 17:     A[Frontend Components] --> B[Layout System]
 18:     A --> C[Chat Interface]
 19:     B --> D[Panel Modes]
 20:     C --> E[Message Management]
 21:     C --> F[AI Integration]
 22:     F --> G[OpenAI API]
 23:     E --> H[State Management]
 24: ```
 25: 
 26: ## Core Components
 27: 
 28: ### 1. Layout System
 29: 
 30: The chat system uses a flexible layout system with multiple display modes:
 31: 
 32: ```typescript
 33: type PanelMode = 'quarter' | 'half' | 'full' | 'floating' | 'icon';
 34: 
 35: interface LayoutProps {
 36:   title: string;
 37:   description?: string;
 38:   chatConfig: ChatConfig;
 39:   rightPanelMode: PanelMode;
 40:   header?: boolean;
 41:   footer?: boolean;
 42: }
 43: ```
 44: 
 45: #### Panel Modes
 46: - `quarter`: 25% width side panel (default)
 47: - `half`: 50% width side panel
 48: - `full`: Full screen interface
 49: - `floating`: Detached window
 50: - `icon`: Minimized button
 51: 
 52: ### 2. Chat Configuration
 53: 
 54: Configure your chat interface using the type-safe schema:
 55: 
 56: ```typescript
 57: const chatConfig = ChatConfigSchema.parse({
 58:   // AI Model Settings
 59:   provider: "openai",
 60:   model: "gpt-4o-mini",
 61:   temperature: 0.7,
 62:   maxTokens: 2000,
 63: 
 64:   // AI Behavior
 65:   systemPrompt: [{
 66:     type: "text",
 67:     text: "Define AI behavior here"
 68:   }],
 69: 
 70:   // User Interface
 71:   welcome: {
 72:     message: "Welcome message",
 73:     avatar: "/path/to/avatar.svg",
 74:     suggestions: [
 75:       {
 76:         label: "Suggestion",
 77:         prompt: "Suggested question"
 78:       }
 79:     ]
 80:   }
 81: });
 82: ```
 83: 
 84: ### 3. Message Management
 85: 
 86: The chat system handles various message types and interactions:
 87: 
 88: ```typescript
 89: interface Message {
 90:   id: string;
 91:   role: 'user' | 'assistant' | 'system';
 92:   content: string;
 93:   timestamp: number;
 94:   metadata?: {
 95:     type?: 'code' | 'markdown' | 'image';
 96:     language?: string;
 97:     voice?: boolean;
 98:   };
 99: }
100: ```
101: 
102: Features:
103: - Real-time streaming
104: - Markdown rendering
105: - Code syntax highlighting
106: - Message history
107: - Voice synthesis
108: - Copy functionality
109: 
110: ### 4. AI Integration
111: 
112: The chat system connects with AI providers through a flexible API layer:
113: 
114: ```typescript
115: interface ChatAPIConfig {
116:   provider: "openai";
117:   model: string;
118:   apiEndpoint: string;
119:   temperature: number;
120:   maxTokens: number;
121:   systemPrompt: SystemPrompt[];
122:   contextData?: string;
123:   functions?: ChatFunction[];
124: }
125: ```
126: 
127: ## Implementation Examples
128: 
129: ### Basic Chat Integration
130: 
131: ```astro
132: ---
133: import Layout from "../layouts/Layout.astro";
134: import { ChatConfigSchema } from '../schema/chat';
135: 
136: const chatConfig = ChatConfigSchema.parse({
137:   systemPrompt: [{
138:     type: "text",
139:     text: "You are a helpful assistant."
140:   }],
141:   welcome: {
142:     message: "How can I help?",
143:     avatar: "/icon.svg"
144:   }
145: });
146: ---
147: 
148: <Layout
149:   title="Chat Example"
150:   chatConfig={chatConfig}
151:   rightPanelMode="quarter"
152: >
153:   <main>Your content here</main>
154: </Layout>
155: ```
156: 
157: ### Advanced Configuration
158: 
159: ```typescript
160: const advancedConfig = {
161:   provider: "openai",
162:   model: "gpt-4o-mini",
163:   temperature: 0.7,
164:   maxTokens: 2000,
165:   features: {
166:     textToSpeech: true,
167:     codeHighlight: true,
168:     markdown: true,
169:     suggestions: true
170:   },
171:   styles: {
172:     theme: "light" | "dark" | "system",
173:     accentColor: "#0066FF",
174:     messageSpacing: "comfortable" | "compact"
175:   }
176: };
177: ```
178: 
179: ## Performance Optimization
180: 
181: ### 1. Edge Runtime
182: 
183: The chat system uses edge computing for optimal performance:
184: 
185: ```typescript
186: // src/pages/api/chat.ts
187: export const config = {
188:   runtime: 'edge',
189:   regions: ['all'],
190: };
191: ```
192: 
193: ### 2. Response Streaming
194: 
195: Implements streaming for real-time responses:
196: 
197: ```typescript
198: const stream = new ReadableStream({
199:   async start(controller) {
200:     const encoder = new TextEncoder();
201:     for await (const chunk of aiResponse) {
202:       controller.enqueue(encoder.encode(chunk));
203:     }
204:     controller.close();
205:   },
206: });
207: ```
208: 
209: ### 3. Caching Strategies
210: 
211: ```typescript
212: // Message caching
213: const messageCache = new Map<string, Message[]>();
214: 
215: // Context caching
216: const contextCache = new LRUCache({
217:   max: 500,
218:   maxAge: 1000 * 60 * 60 // 1 hour
219: });
220: ```
221: 
222: ## Best Practices
223: 
224: 1. **System Prompt Design**
225:    - Be specific about AI role
226:    - Include necessary context
227:    - Set clear boundaries
228:    - Define response format
229: 
230: 2. **Error Handling**
231:    ```typescript
232:    try {
233:      const response = await chat.sendMessage(message);
234:    } catch (error) {
235:      if (error.code === 'context_length_exceeded') {
236:        // Handle context length
237:      } else if (error.code === 'rate_limit_exceeded') {
238:        // Handle rate limiting
239:      }
240:      // Handle other errors
241:    }
242:    ```
243: 
244: 3. **Memory Management**
245:    - Implement conversation pruning
246:    - Use efficient data structures
247:    - Clean up unused resources
248: 
249: ## Troubleshooting
250: 
251: Common issues and solutions:
252: 
253: 1. **Performance Issues**
254:    - Enable edge runtime
255:    - Implement proper caching
256:    - Optimize message size
257:    - Use streaming responses
258: 
259: 2. **API Errors**
260:    - Verify API keys
261:    - Check rate limits
262:    - Monitor usage quotas
263:    - Handle timeouts
264: 
265: 3. **UI Problems**
266:    - Check panel mode
267:    - Verify CSS classes
268:    - Test responsiveness
269:    - Monitor console errors
`````

## File: src/content/docs/development/custom-agents.md
`````markdown
  1: ---
  2: title: Creating Custom AI Agents
  3: description: Learn to build specialized AI agents with custom capabilities
  4: date: 2024-02-02
  5: section: Tutorials
  6: order: 1
  7: ---
  8: 
  9: # Creating Custom AI Agents
 10: 
 11: Learn how to create specialized AI agents with custom capabilities, system prompts, and advanced features. This tutorial will show you how to build agents for specific use cases.
 12: 
 13: ## Use Cases
 14: 
 15: We'll create three different types of agents:
 16: 1. Documentation Assistant
 17: 2. Product Support Agent
 18: 3. Content Generation Agent
 19: 
 20: ## Documentation Assistant
 21: 
 22: ### Step 1: Basic Setup
 23: 
 24: ```astro
 25: ---
 26: import Layout from "../layouts/Layout.astro";
 27: import { ChatConfigSchema } from '../schema/chat';
 28: 
 29: // Get documentation content
 30: const docs = await Astro.glob('../content/docs/**/*.md');
 31: const docsContent = docs.map(doc => ({
 32:   title: doc.frontmatter.title,
 33:   content: doc.rawContent(),
 34:   url: doc.url
 35: }));
 36: 
 37: const chatConfig = ChatConfigSchema.parse({
 38:   systemPrompt: [{
 39:     type: "text",
 40:     text: `You are a documentation expert for our platform.
 41:     Your knowledge base includes:
 42:     ${docsContent.map(doc => `
 43:       # ${doc.title}
 44:       ${doc.content}
 45:     `).join('\n')}
 46:     
 47:     Guidelines:
 48:     1. Reference specific documentation pages when answering
 49:     2. Provide code examples when relevant
 50:     3. Suggest related documentation
 51:     4. Guide users through complex topics step by step`
 52:   }],
 53:   welcome: {
 54:     message: "👋 I can help you find and understand our documentation. What would you like to know?",
 55:     avatar: "/docs-icon.svg",
 56:     suggestions: [
 57:       {
 58:         label: "Getting Started",
 59:         prompt: "What's the best way to get started?"
 60:       },
 61:       {
 62:         label: "Find Topic",
 63:         prompt: "Can you help me find documentation about..."
 64:       }
 65:     ]
 66:   }
 67: });
 68: ---
 69: 
 70: <Layout
 71:   title="Documentation Assistant"
 72:   chatConfig={chatConfig}
 73:   rightPanelMode="quarter"
 74: >
 75:   <main class="prose max-w-4xl mx-auto p-8">
 76:     <h1>Documentation Assistant</h1>
 77:     <p>Ask me anything about our documentation!</p>
 78:   </main>
 79: </Layout>
 80: ```
 81: 
 82: ## Product Support Agent
 83: 
 84: ### Step 1: Define Knowledge Base

100:       a: "Detailed answer..."
101:     }
102:   ],
103:   procedures: [

105:       title: "How to...",

107:     }

166: ## Content Generation Agent
167: 
168: ### Step 1: Define Content Types
169: 
170: ```typescript
171: // src/types/content.ts
172: export interface ContentTemplate {
173:   type: 'blog' | 'social' | 'email';
174:   structure: string[];
175:   tone: 'professional' | 'casual' | 'technical';

183:     tone: 'professional',
184:     length: 'long'
185:   },
186:   tweetThread: {

188:     structure: ['Hook', 'Key Points', 'Call to Action'],
189:     tone: 'casual',
190:     length: 'short'
191:   }
192: };

194: 
195: ### Step 2: Create Content Agent
196: 
197: ```astro

204:   systemPrompt: [{
205:     type: "text",
206:     text: `You are a content generation expert.

210:

213:     2. Adapt tone and style as needed
214:     3. Optimize for different platforms
215:     4. Maintain brand voice
216:     
217:     Guidelines:
218:     - Follow SEO best practices
219:     - Maintain consistent tone
220:     - Include relevant keywords
221:     - Adapt length appropriately`
222:   }],
223:   welcome: {
224:     message: "Ready to help you create engaging content! What would you like to create?",
225:     avatar: "/content-icon.svg",
226:     suggestions: [
227:       {
228:         label: "Blog Post",
229:         prompt: "Help me write a blog post about..."
230:       },
231:       {
232:         label: "Tweet Thread",
233:         prompt: "Create a tweet thread about..."
234:       }
235:     ]
236:   },
237:   features: {
238:     markdown: true,
239:     codeHighlight: true
240:   }
241: });
242: ---
243: 
244: <Layout
245:   title="Content Generator"
246:   chatConfig={chatConfig}
247:   rightPanelMode="half"
248: >
249:   <!-- Content generation interface -->
250: </Layout>
251: ```
252: 
253: ## Best Practices
254: 
255: 1. **System Prompt Design**
256:    - Be specific about the agent's role
257:    - Include relevant knowledge
258:    - Define clear boundaries
259:    - Specify output formats
260: 
261: 2. **Knowledge Organization**
262:    - Structure data clearly
263:    - Update content regularly
264:    - Include examples
265:    - Maintain consistency
266: 
267: 3. **User Experience**
268:    - Provide relevant suggestions
269:    - Include helpful examples
270:    - Offer clear instructions
271:    - Handle errors gracefully
272: 
273: ## Advanced Features
274: 
275: ### 1. Context Awareness
276: 
277: ```typescript
278: // Add page context to your agent
279: const pageContext = {
280:   currentPage: Astro.url.pathname,
281:   userPreferences: getUserPreferences(),
282:   recentInteractions: getRecentHistory()
283: };
284: 
285: const contextAwareConfig = {
286:   ...chatConfig,
287:   contextData: JSON.stringify(pageContext)
288: };
289: ```
290: 
291: ### 2. Multi-step Tasks
292: 
293: ```typescript
294: // Define task workflows
295: const workflows = {
296:   contentCreation: [
297:     { step: 'gather_requirements', prompt: 'What type of content do you need?' },
298:     { step: 'generate_outline', prompt: 'Here\'s the proposed outline:' },
299:     { step: 'create_content', prompt: 'Generating content based on outline...' },
300:     { step: 'review', prompt: 'Please review the generated content:' }
301:   ]
302: };
303: ```
`````

## File: src/content/docs/development/testing-with-vitest.md
`````markdown
  1: ---
  2: title: Testing with Vitest
  3: description: A comprehensive guide to setting up and running tests with Vitest in an Astro project
  4: date: 2024-02-18
  5: section: Development
  6: order: 6
  7: ---
  8: 
  9: # Testing with Vitest in Astro
 10: 
 11: This guide will walk you through setting up and running tests with Vitest in your Astro project.
 12: 
 13: ## Step 1: Install Dependencies
 14: 
 15: First, install Vitest and related testing libraries:
 16: 
 17: ```bash
 18: pnpm add -D vitest @testing-library/react @testing-library/jest-dom happy-dom @types/node @vitejs/plugin-react
 19: ```
 20: 
 21: These packages provide:
 22: - `vitest`: The testing framework
 23: - `@testing-library/react`: Utilities for testing React components
 24: - `@testing-library/jest-dom`: Custom jest matchers for DOM testing
 25: - `happy-dom`: A lightweight browser environment for testing
 26: - `@vitejs/plugin-react`: React support for Vite/Vitest
 27: 
 28: ## Step 2: Create Vitest Configuration
 29: 
 30: Create a `vitest.config.ts` file in your project root:
 31: 
 32: ```typescript
 33: /// <reference types="vitest" />
 34: import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
 35: import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
 36: 
 37: export default defineConfig({
 38:   plugins: [react()],
 39:   test: {
 40:     environment: 'happy-dom',
 41:     globals: true,
 42:     setupFiles: './src/test/setup.ts',
 43:     include: ['**/*.{test,spec}.{js,mjs,cjs,ts,mts,cts,jsx,tsx}'],
 44:     exclude: ['node_modules', 'dist', '.idea', '.git', '.cache']
 45:   }
 46: });
 47: ```
 48: 
 49: ## Step 3: Create Test Setup File
 50: 
 51: Create a test setup file at `src/test/setup.ts`:
 52: 
 53: ```typescript
 54: import '@testing-library/jest-dom';
 55: import { cleanup } from '@testing-library/react';
 56: import { afterEach } from 'vitest';
 57: 
 58: // Cleanup after each test
 59: afterEach(() => {
 60:   cleanup();
 61: });
 62: ```
 63: 
 64: ## Step 4: Update Package.json Scripts
 65: 
 66: Add test scripts to your package.json:
 67: 
 68: ```json
 69: {
 70:   "scripts": {
 71:     "test": "vitest",
 72:     "test:ui": "vitest --ui",
 73:     "test:run": "vitest run",
 74:     "coverage": "vitest run --coverage"
 75:   }
 76: }
 77: ```
 78: 
 79: ## Step 5: Writing Your First Test
 80: 
 81: Create a test file for a component. For example, `src/components/ModeToggle.test.tsx`:
 82: 
 83: ```typescript
 84: import { describe, expect, it } from 'vitest';
 85: import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
 86: import { ModeToggle } from './ModeToggle';
 87: import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
 88: 
 89: describe('ModeToggle', () => {
 90:   it('renders the toggle button', () => {
 91:     render(<ModeToggle />);
 92:     const button = screen.getByRole('button');
 93:     expect(button).toBeInTheDocument();
 94:   });
 95: 
 96:   it('changes theme when clicked', async () => {
 97:     render(<ModeToggle />);
 98:     const button = screen.getByRole('button');
 99:     
100:     await userEvent.click(button);
101:     expect(document.documentElement.classList).toContain('dark');
102:   });
103: });
104: ```
105: 
106: ## Step 6: Running Tests
107: 
108: You can run tests using several commands:
109: 
110: 1. Run tests in watch mode (development):
111: ```bash
112: pnpm test
113: ```
114: 
115: 2. Run tests once (CI/CD):
116: ```bash
117: pnpm test:run
118: ```
119: 
120: 3. Run tests with UI interface:
121: ```bash
122: pnpm test:ui
123: ```
124: 
125: 4. Generate coverage report:
126: ```bash
127: pnpm coverage
128: ```
129: 
130: ## Test Structure Best Practices
131: 
132: 1. **File Organization**:
133:    - Place test files next to the components they test
134:    - Use `.test.tsx` or `.spec.tsx` suffix
135:    - Group related tests in describe blocks
136: 
137: 2. **Naming Conventions**:
138:    - Use descriptive test names
139:    - Follow the pattern: "it should [expected behavior]"
140:    - Group related tests in meaningful describe blocks
141: 
142: 3. **Testing Patterns**:
143: ```typescript
144: describe('Component', () => {
145:   // Setup/teardown hooks if needed
146:   beforeEach(() => {
147:     // Setup code
148:   });
149: 
150:   afterEach(() => {
151:     // Cleanup code
152:   });
153: 
154:   // Test cases
155:   it('should render correctly', () => {
156:     // Test implementation
157:   });
158: 
159:   it('should handle user interaction', async () => {
160:     // Test implementation
161:   });
162: });
163: ```
164: 
165: ## Common Testing Utilities
166: 
167: 1. **Rendering Components**:
168: ```typescript
169: import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
170: 
171: render(<YourComponent />);
172: ```
173: 
174: 2. **Finding Elements**:
175: ```typescript
176: // By role
177: const button = screen.getByRole('button');
178: 
179: // By text
180: const element = screen.getByText('Hello');
181: 
182: // By test ID
183: const custom = screen.getByTestId('custom-element');
184: ```
185: 
186: 3. **User Interactions**:
187: ```typescript
188: import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
189: 
190: await userEvent.click(button);
191: await userEvent.type(input, 'Hello');
192: ```
193: 
194: 4. **Assertions**:
195: ```typescript
196: expect(element).toBeInTheDocument();
197: expect(element).toHaveTextContent('Hello');
198: expect(element).toBeVisible();
199: ```
200: 
201: ## Debugging Tests
202: 
203: 1. Use the UI interface for better debugging:
204: ```bash
205: pnpm test:ui
206: ```
207: 
208: 2. Use console.log in tests:
209: ```typescript
210: it('should work', () => {
211:   console.log('Debug info:', someValue);
212:   expect(true).toBe(true);
213: });
214: ```
215: 
216: 3. Use the debug utility:
217: ```typescript
218: import { screen } from '@testing-library/react';
219: 
220: screen.debug();
221: ```
222: 
223: Remember to write tests that focus on behavior rather than implementation details, and aim for high test coverage of critical application logic.
`````

  1: ---
  2: title: Getting Started with ONE
  3: description: Learn how to set up and start building with the ONE framework
